claims.text: The balance between configurational entropy and surface energy determines the structural and chemical stability of high-entropy nanoalloys at high temperature.
Minimizing surface energy through controlled rapid thermal ramping or compositional tuning allows configurational entropy to suppress atomic segregation.
Suppression of atomic segregation preserves the disordered phase.
Slower heating or increased surface exposure causes surface-energy effects to dominate.
Dominant surface-energy effects promote localized atomic reordering and clustering.
Localized atomic reordering and clustering can lead to chemical instability.
The proposed initial material is a nanoscale multi-principal-element alloy with a single-phase disordered or metastable structure at room temperature.
Nanoscale surface and interfacial regions mediate atomic-reordering events through their energy state.
At high temperature, high configurational entropy favors a kinetically stabilized disordered state.
Slower heating or longer dwell times enhance surface energy.
Enhanced surface energy drives atomic diffusion toward clustering and local ordering.
Clustering and local ordering lead to incipient phase separation.
Rapid thermal ramping will maintain the disordered structure with minimal atomic clustering.
Slower heating will produce more atomic reordering and clustering at surfaces or interfaces than rapid heating.
Longer dwell times will produce more atomic reordering and clustering at surfaces or interfaces than the rapid-ramp baseline.
A rapidly heated high-entropy nanoalloy provides a baseline in which configurational entropy suppresses observable clustering and maintains a disordered phase.
The prediction applies only within the studied compositional regime and below the onset of irreversible phase transitions or melting.

A lack of significant differences in clustering, ordering, or phase-transition behavior between nominally surface-energy-modulating conditions and the rapid-ramp baseline would falsify the proposed mechanism.
